Neither candidate instrument in the dataset supports a credible instrumental-variables design, so we cannot estimate the causal effect using standard 2SLS on this sample. The first candidate, `monsoon_dev` (percent deviation in monsoon rainfall), has a strong first stage with district and year fixed effects, but it violates the exclusion restriction because districts downstream of irrigation dams—where crop income is insulated from local rainfall—experience the same increase in riots during dry years, indicating direct non-income channels (such as water scarcity or temperature stress). The second candidate, `works_draw` (a randomized public-works lottery in one state from 1993–1995), satisfies independence and exclusion, but it is only defined for 48 district-years and suffers from a severely weak first stage ($F \approx 2$). Because conventional IV estimation with `works_draw` would be heavily biased and underpowered, the best available credible strategy is to restrict the sample to the 16 lottery districts in 1993–1995 and report intention-to-treat (reduced-form) effects and weak-IV-robust Anderson-Rubin confidence sets using `works_draw`, while controlling for baseline 1981 covariates (`pop_1981`, `muslim_share`, `urban_share`, `literacy`, `riots_prev`) to improve precision. The main threat to this fallback strategy is severe statistical imprecision, as the tiny subsample and 0.2 percentage-point first stage will yield wide confidence intervals that are unlikely to be informative.

works_draw | doubtful

We cannot credibly estimate the causal effect of rural income growth on Hindu-Muslim riots with this dataset because neither of the two candidate instrumental variables is valid. The first candidate, `monsoon_dev` (percent deviation of monsoon rainfall), violates the exclusion restriction: the documentation notes that dam-irrigated districts—where canal water keeps crop income unchanged across monsoons—experience just as large an increase in riots during deficit monsoon years (`monsoon_dev` < -10%) as other districts, proving rainfall affects riots through non-income channels (such as direct heat/water stress or relief manual declarations). The second candidate, `works_draw` (a randomized public-works lottery), satisfies exogeneity and exclusion, but it is a severely weak instrument with a first-stage F-statistic of about 2 and is only non-missing for 16 districts in a single state from 1993–1995 (48 observations). Because 2SLS with `works_draw` would suffer from severe weak-instrument bias and `monsoon_dev` is invalid, no credible instrumental variable strategy is available. The best remaining option with the full panel is a two-way fixed effects regression controlling for district and year fixed effects (or interacting baseline 1981 covariates like `pop_1981`, `muslim_share`, `urban_share`, `literacy`, and `riots_prev` with year effects), while reporting the `works_draw` reduced-form intent-to-treat effect and Anderson-Rubin weak-IV confidence intervals on the 16-district subsample as a supplementary check. The main threat to the panel fixed-effects approach is time-varying omitted variable bias and reverse causality, as unobserved local shocks or outbreaks of violence may simultaneously disrupt rural economic activity and drive riot counts.

We cannot credibly estimate the causal effect of rural income growth on Hindu-Muslim riots with an instrumental-variables design in this dataset because neither candidate instrument is valid. The first candidate, `monsoon_dev` (monsoon rainfall deviation), violates the exclusion restriction: the program documentation notes that districts downstream of irrigation dams—where canal water keeps crop income unchanged across monsoons—experience roughly the same increase in riots during deficit monsoon years as other districts, proving rainfall affects riots through non-income channels (such as heat, water stress, or relief-manual administrative designations). The second candidate, `works_draw` (the 1992 random lottery for a rural public-works program), satisfies random assignment and the exclusion restriction, but it is only defined for 16 districts in a single state from 1993 to 1995 and has a first-stage F-statistic of about 2, making it a severely weak instrument. Relying on `monsoon_dev` would yield biased estimates due to the direct effect of monsoon deficits on conflict, while relying on `works_draw` would produce unreliable estimates with severe weak-instrument bias and insufficient statistical power. Consequently, rather than reporting a spurious 2SLS estimate, we should report the reduced-form effect of the public-works lottery (`works_draw`) on riots in the 16-district subsample and use weak-instrument-robust inference (such as Anderson-Rubin confidence sets) to bound the treatment effect. In the full 290-district panel, we are limited to two-way fixed effects regressions (controlling for district and year fixed effects, or state-by-year fixed effects and baseline 1981 characteristics like `pop_1981`, `muslim_share`, `urban_share`, `literacy`, and `riots_prev` interacted with time trends), while explicitly acknowledging that time-varying unobserved shocks prevent a strict causal interpretation.

Neither of the two candidate instruments in the dataset provides a credible instrumental-variables design to estimate the causal effect of rural income growth on Hindu-Muslim riots. The first candidate, `monsoon_dev` (monsoon rainfall deviation), violates the exclusion restriction because districts downstream of irrigation dams—where canal water insulates crop income from monsoon fluctuations—experience just as large an increase in riots during dry years as rain-fed districts, demostrarating that rainfall affects riots through non-income channels. The second candidate, `works_draw` (the 1992 random assignment of a rural public-works program), satisfies exogeneity and exclusion, but it is only defined for 16 districts over three years and has a first-stage F-statistic of about 2, making it too weak for valid two-stage least squares inference. Because no valid and sufficiently strong instrument is available in the data, we cannot credibly point-identify the causal effect of rural income growth using an instrumental variables strategy. Instead, we can only report the reduced-form intent-to-treat effect of `works_draw` on riots in the 16-district subsample (using weak-instrument-robust Anderson-Rubin confidence intervals if scaling by income growth) and present panel fixed-effects regressions (controlling for district and year fixed effects, or state-by-year fixed effects and baseline 1981 characteristics like `pop_1981`, `muslim_share`, `urban_share`, `literacy`, and `riots_prev` interacted with time trends) as descriptive, non-causal associations. The main threat to any panel regression approach is time-varying omitted variables—such as local political shocks or unmeasured weather stress—that simultaneously depress rural economic activity and trigger communal violence, while the `works_draw` subsample analysis is severely limited by low statistical power and weak-instrument bias.

INSTRUMENT: NONE

To estimate the causal effect of annual rural income per person growth on the number of Hindu-Muslim riots, I will use an instrumental variables (2SLS) design across the panel of 290 districts from 1982 to 1995. I will instrument for district rural income growth using `monsoon_dev`, the percent deviation of the district's June-September monsoon rainfall from its 1951-1980 historical average. Conditional on district and year fixed effects, year-to-year rainfall deviations provide exogenous weather shocks that strongly shift agricultural income (raising rural income growth by 1.6 percentage points per 10-point increase). I will also evaluate `works_draw` (a randomized public-works lottery in one state from 1993-1995), but reject it as the primary instrument because it covers only a tiny subsample (48 district-years) and suffers from severe weak-instrument bias (first-stage F-statistic of about 2). In addition to district and year fixed effects, I can interact the 1981 baseline covariates (`pop_1981`, `muslim_share`, `urban_share`, `literacy`, and `riots_prev`) with year indicators for robustness, while clustering standard errors at the district level. The main threat to identification is a violation of the exclusion restriction: extreme monsoon rainfall or flooding might directly affect riot counts through non-income channels, such as physically impeding street gatherings or straining local infrastructure and policing.

CANDIDATES:
monsoon_dev | plausible
works_draw | doubtful
INSTRUMENT: monsoon_dev

We cannot credibly estimate the causal effect of rural income growth on Hindu-Muslim riots using an instrumental-variables design in this dataset because both candidate instruments fail key identification requirements. The first candidate, `monsoon_dev` (monsoon rainfall deviation, used with district and year fixed effects), violates the exclusion restriction: program documentation shows that in deficit monsoon years, riots increase just as much in dam-irrigated districts where canal water keeps crop income unchanged, proving that rainfall affects riots through non-income channels. The second candidate, `works_draw` (the 1992 random lottery assigning a rural public-works program across 16 districts in 1993–1995), satisfies exogeneity and exclusion, as the lottery was random and changed nothing else in drawn districts. However, `works_draw` suffers from a severely weak first stage (an F-statistic of about 2 and only 0.2 percentage points higher income growth across 48 district-year observations), which would yield heavily biased and uninformative 2SLS estimates. Without a valid and strong instrument, we are limited to a two-way fixed effects panel regression of district-year riots on rural income growth controlling for district and year fixed effects (or interacting baseline 1981 covariates `pop_1981`, `muslim_share`, `urban_share`, `literacy`, and `riots_prev` with year effects), alongside reporting the reduced-form intent-to-treat effect of `works_draw`. The main threat to this fallback panel strategy is time-varying omitted variables and reverse causality—such as local political or economic shocks that simultaneously depress rural income growth and trigger communal violence—which cannot be resolved without a valid instrument.

To estimate the causal effect of district rural income growth on the number of Hindu-Muslim riots, I will use an instrumental variables (2SLS) strategy across the full panel of 290 districts from 1982 to 1995. I will instrument for annual rural income growth using `monsoon_dev`, the percent deviation of the district's June–September monsoon rainfall from its 1951–1980 historical average. Because rainfall deviations are realizations of weather around a district's long-run norm, they provide plausibly exogenous variation in agricultural output and rural income when conditioning on district and year fixed effects, with a strong first stage (a 10-point increase raises rural income growth by 1.6 percentage points). I will include district fixed effects to absorb time-invariant district characteristics—or interact baseline 1981 controls (`pop_1981`, `muslim_share`, `urban_share`, `literacy`, and `riots_prev`) with time trends for robustness—alongside year fixed effects and cluster standard errors at the district level. I reject the alternative candidate instrument `works_draw` (the 1992 public-works lottery) because it is only defined for 16 districts in 1993–1995 and suffers from a severe weak-instrument problem (first-stage F-statistic of about 2). The main threat to the `monsoon_dev` design is a violation of the exclusion restriction: extreme rainfall or flooding could directly affect the logistics of collective violence, crowd gathering, or policing independent of rural income growth.

The second candidate, `works_draw` (the 1992 randomized public-works lottery), satisfies exogeneity and exclusion, but it is only defined for 16 districts over three years and suffers from severe weak-instrument bias with a first-stage F-statistic of about 2. Consequently, there is no valid and sufficiently strong instrument available in this dataset to support an instrumental variables design. As a fallback, we can estimate a two-way fixed effects panel regression of district-year riot counts on rural income growth with district and year fixed effects (or state-by-year fixed effects and 1981 baseline characteristics interacted with time trends), while reporting reduced-form intent-to-treat estimates for `works_draw` as supplementary evidence. The main threat to this panel strategy is time-varying omitted variables and reverse causality, such as local political shocks orincipient communal tensions that simultaneously disrupt rural economic activity and trigger riots.

To estimate the causal effect of district rural income growth on Hindu-Muslim riots, I will use an instrumental variables (2SLS) design. I will instrument for the treatment (annual percent growth of district rural income per person) using `monsoon_dev`, the percent deviation of June-September monsoon rainfall from the district's 1951–1980 historical average, while the outcome is the number of Hindu-Muslim riots in the district-year. Following the codebook documentation, the specification will include district and year fixed effects ( absorbing time-invariant baseline characteristics like `pop_1981`, `muslim_share`, `urban_share`, `literacy`, and `riots_prev`, though these can be interacted with time trends for robustness) and cluster standard errors at the district level. `monsoon_dev` provides a strong and quasi-random first stage across the full sample, whereas the alternative candidate `works_draw` is a weak instrument (first-stage F-statistic of about 2) available only for 16 districts in 1993–1995. The main threat to identification is a violation of the exclusion restriction: extreme rainfall shocks could directly affect riot counts through channels other than rural income growth, such as physically hindering street gatherings or disrupting transport and policing during floods.

To estimate the causal effect of county voter turnout on the incumbent party's presidential vote share, we cannot rely on a standard instrumental variables design across the full panel because neither candidate instrument in the dataset is both valid and strong. Specifically, election-day rainfall (`eday_rain`) has a strong first stage under county and election-year fixed effects, but it violates the exclusion restriction because rain directly increases risk aversion and pro-incumbent voting even among inframarginal voters who would have turned out regardless of the weather. The randomized nonpartisan postcard reminder (`reminder_draw`) satisfies random assignment and the exclusion restriction, but it is available for only 180 county-elections in the 1996–2000 three-state pilot and suffers from a weak first stage ($F \approx 4$), making two-stage least squares biased and unreliable. Consequently, I recommend not using an instrument (`NONE`) for the main 1948–2000 analysis, instead estimating a two-way fixed effects panel regression with county and state-by-year (or election-year) fixed effects while controlling for predetermined county covariates (`dem_prev`, `pop_density`, `pct_rural`, and `median_inc`). As a supplementary design-based check on the 180-observation pilot subsample, we can report the intent-to-treat (reduced-form) effect of `reminder_draw` on incumbent vote share and construct weak-instrument-robust Anderson–Rubin confidence intervals. The main threat to identification in the panel specification is time-varying, county-specific unobserved shocks—such as local campaign mobilization or economic shifts—that simultaneously alter turnout and partisan preferences.

CANDIDATES:
eday_rain | violated
reminder_draw | doubtful
INSTRUMENT: NONE

I propose an instrumental variables (2SLS) strategy using election-day rainfall (`eday_rain`) as an instrument for county voter turnout (`Treatment`) to estimate its causal effect on the incumbent party's vote share (`Outcome`). Because `eday_rain` is defined as the deviation from the county's long-run average election-day rainfall and the model includes county and election-year fixed effects, the instrument exploits idiosyncratic weather shocks that are plausibly exogenous to local political preferences. The first stage is strong across the full sample of 3,100 counties over 14 elections, with each additional inch of rain reducing turnout by 1.1 percentage points. To improve precision and account for observable time-varying county characteristics, I will also control for `dem_prev`, `pop_density`, `pct_rural`, and `median_inc`, and cluster standard errors at the county (or `state`) level. I reject the alternative candidate instrument `reminder_draw` because it is only available for a tiny subsample of 180 county-elections and suffers from a severe weak-instrument problem (first-stage F-statistic of about 4). The main threat to our identification strategy is a potential exclusion restriction violation if election-day rain directly alters voters' mood or incumbent evaluations, or if rainfall is spatially correlated with unobservable regional shocks that simultaneously affect voting behavior.

CANDIDATES:
eday_rain | plausible
reminder_draw | doubtful
INSTRUMENT: eday_rain

Neither candidate instrument in the dataset supports a credible instrumental-variables design for the full 1948–2000 sample. Election-day rainfall (`eday_rain`) has a strong first stage, but it violates the exclusion restriction because post-election surveys show that rain directly reduces risk tolerance among always-takers and shifts their votes toward the incumbent party independent of turnout. The randomized nonpartisan mailer (`reminder_draw`) satisfies independence and exclusion, but it is only available for a 180-observation pilot subsample (1996–2000) and suffers from a weak first stage ($F \approx 4$), making standard 2SLS biased and imprecise. Consequently, for the full panel of 3,100 counties, I recommend a two-way fixed effects (difference-in-differences) regression of incumbent party vote share on county turnout, controlling for county and election-year fixed effects as well as time-varying county covariates (`dem_prev`, `pop_density`, `pct_rural`, `median_inc`, and state-by-year interactions using `state` and `south` to absorb state-level polling and absentee rule changes). We can complement this full-sample panel specification with weak-instrument-robust Anderson–Rubin confidence intervals using `reminder_draw` in the 180-observation pilot subsample as a local check. The main threat to the panel strategy is time-varying unobserved county shocks—such as local economic downturns or divisive ballot initiatives—that simultaneously mobilize voters and shift preferences toward or against the incumbent president's party.

CANDIDATES:
eday_rain | violated
reminder_draw | doubtful
INSTRUMENT: NONE

To estimate the causal effect of county voter turnout on the incumbent party's presidential vote share, I evaluated two potential instrumental variables in the dataset, `eday_rain` and `reminder_draw`, and concluded that neither supports a credible instrumental variables strategy. Election-day rainfall (`eday_rain`) strongly shifts turnout conditional on county and election-year fixed effects, but it violates the exclusion restriction because post-election surveys show that rain directly increases risk aversion among inframarginal voters and causes them to favor the incumbent party regardless of turnout. The randomized nonpartisan mailed reminder (`reminder_draw`) satisfies independence and exclusion, but it is a weak instrument (first-stage $F \approx 4$) and is only observed for a tiny pilot subsample of 180 county-elections in three states from 1996 to 2000. Because no valid and sufficiently powered instrument is available for the full sample, we should not rely on two-stage least squares (though one could report Anderson-Rubin weak-IV-robust confidence intervals for the 180-observation `reminder_draw` subsample as a noisy benchmark). Instead, the best available specification on the full panel is a two-way fixed effects regression of incumbent vote share on turnout, controlling for county and election-year fixed effects (`state`-by-year trends or `south`-by-year interactions) and time-varying county covariates (`dem_prev`, `pop_density`, `pct_rural`, and `median_inc`). The main threat to this fallback strategy is time-varying unobserved confounding—such as local campaign mobilization or economic shocks—that simultaneously alters county turnout and partisan voting preferences, as well as Nickell bias from including lagged vote share (`dem_prev`).

CANDIDATES:
eday_rain | violated
reminder_draw | doubtful
INSTRUMENT: NONE

I will estimate the causal effect of county voter turnout on the incumbent party's presidential vote share using a two-stage least squares (2SLS) instrumental variables design across the panel of U.S. counties from 1948 to 2000. The endogenous treatment is county turnout (in percentage points of the voting-age population), the outcome is the incumbent party's county vote share, and the instrument is `eday_rain`, which measures election-day rainfall as a deviation from the county's long-run election-day average. In both stages, I will include county and election-year fixed effects so that identification comes from within-county, idiosyncratic weather shocks, and I will control for time-varying county covariates (`dem_prev`, `pop_density`, `pct_rural`, and `median_inc`) while clustering standard errors at the county (or state) level. `eday_rain` provides a strong first stage—lowering turnout by 1.1 percentage points per inch—and is plausibly exogenous conditional on county and year fixed effects. I will not use `reminder_draw` as an instrument because it is only available for a small pilot subsample of 180 county-elections and suffers from a weak first stage ($F \approx 4$). The main threat to identification is a violation of the exclusion restriction if election-day rain affects the incumbent's vote share through channels other than overall turnout, such as by directly altering voter mood toward the incumbent or by changing the partisan composition of the electorate.

CANDIDATES:
eday_rain | plausible
reminder_draw | doubtful
INSTRUMENT: eday_rain

I will instrument for endogenous county turnout using `eday_rain`, the deviation of election-day rainfall from the county's long-run election-day average, which strongly reduces turnout by 1.1 percentage points per inch. The specification will include county and election-year fixed effects alongside time-varying county covariates (`dem_prev`, `pop_density`, `pct_rural`, and `median_inc`), clustering standard errors at the county or state level. I will not use `reminder_draw` as an instrument because it is only available for 180 county-elections and suffers from a weak first stage (F-statistic of about 4). Conditional on county and election-year fixed effects, election-day rainfall deviations provide quasi-random weather shocks across the full sample. The main threat to identification is a violation of the exclusion restriction if election-day rain directly alters voter moods toward the incumbent or differentially deters specific partisan subgroups, thereby changing the partisan composition of the electorate independent of overall turnout levels.

To estimate the causal effect of county voter turnout on the incumbent president's party vote share, neither candidate instrument in the dataset supports a credible instrumental variables strategy across the full sample. While election-day rainfall (`eday_rain`) strongly predicts turnout conditional on county and election-year fixed effects, the program documentation reveals an exclusion restriction violation: wet polling days directly reduce voters' willingness to take risks and increase support for the incumbent party among those who vote. The randomized nonpartisan reminder pilot (`reminder_draw`) satisfies independence and exclusion, but it is only available for 180 county-elections in 1996–2000 and suffers from a weak first stage ($F \approx 4$), making standard two-stage least squares unreliable. Consequently, the most credible available approach is a two-way fixed effects panel regression (controlling for county and election-year fixed effects along with time-varying covariates `dem_prev`, `pop_density`, `pct_rural`, and `median_inc`), supplemented by weak-instrument-robust Anderson-Rubin confidence intervals using `reminder_draw` on the 180-observation experimental subsample. The main threat to identification in the panel specification is time-varying unobserved confounding—such as local campaign mobilization or economic shocks—while the experimental subsample faces severe imprecise estimation and limited external validity.

We do not have a credible instrumental variables strategy in this dataset to estimate the causal effect of county turnout on the incumbent party's vote share across the full sample. The primary candidate instrument, `eday_rain` (election-day rainfall deviation, conditional on county and year fixed effects), has a strong first stage, but the program documentation notes that wet polling days (>0.1 inch of rain) directly induce risk aversion among always-taker voters, causing them to favor the incumbent candidate and violating the exclusion restriction. The alternative candidate, `reminder_draw` (random assignment to a nonpartisan mailed election reminder), satisfies random assignment and the exclusion restriction because it named no candidate or party and changed nothing else in drawn counties. However, `reminder_draw` is only available for a tiny pilot subsample of 180 county-elections and suffers from a severe weak-instrument problem, with a first-stage F-statistic of about 4. Because `eday_rain` is invalid and `reminder_draw` is too weak and limited in scope for reliable two-stage least squares estimation, neither variable can serve as a standalone instrument for the full study. If we restrict our focus to the 1996–2000 three-state pilot subsample, we can report intention-to-treat (reduced-form) effects of `reminder_draw` and use weak-instrument-robust inference (such as Anderson-Rubin confidence intervals), though statistical power will remain severely limited.

There is no credible instrumental-variables strategy in this dataset to estimate the causal effect of county turnout on the incumbent party's vote share. The primary candidate instrument, election-day rainfall (`eday_rain`), has a strong first stage conditional on county and year fixed effects, but it violates the exclusion restriction. Specifically, the program documentation reveals that voting on a wet polling day (>0.1 inch of rain) directly reduces voters' willingness to take risks and increases their support for the incumbent party among those who already turn out. The alternative candidate, the randomized nonpartisan mailed reminder (`reminder_draw`), satisfies independence and exclusion because it was randomly assigned and named no candidate or party. However, `reminder_draw` is only available for a 180-observation pilot subsample and suffers from a weak first stage ($F \approx 4$), making two-stage least squares estimates severely biased and imprecise. Consequently, any analysis would have to rely on two-way fixed effects controlling for `dem_prev`, `pop_density`, `pct_rural`, and `median_inc`, where the main threat to identification is time-varying unobserved county shocks—such as local campaign intensity or economic shifts—that simultaneously drive both turnout and incumbent support.

To estimate the effect of racial residential segregation on city direct general expenditure per resident, I recommend against an instrumental variables strategy because neither candidate instrument in the dataset is credible. The first candidate, `waterways`, violates the exclusion restriction because every boundary stream in the 1920 survey became a jurisdictional line, meaning more waterways directly fragment metropolitan areas into more separately governed municipalities and school districts, which independently alters local public spending responsibilities and fiscal competition. The second candidate, `audit_grant`, satisfies exogeneity and exclusion through random assignment to nonprofits, but it is only available for 40 cities and suffers from severe weak-instrument bias with a first-stage F-statistic of about 2. Instead, we should leverage the 1980–2010 panel structure using a two-way fixed effects specification with city and state-by-year fixed effects. In this model, we regress per-resident expenditure on the multigroup entropy segregation index while controlling for time-varying city covariates (`log_pop`, `pct_black`, `pct_hisp`, `med_income`, and `own_rate`). The main threat to this identification strategy is time-varying, within-city unobserved confounding—such as local economic shocks or fiscal crises—that simultaneously drives residential sorting and municipal budget decisions, as well as potential reverse causality from public spending to residential location choices.

CANDIDATES:
waterways | violated
audit_grant | doubtful
INSTRUMENT: NONE

Neither candidate instrument in the dataset supports a credible instrumental-variables design. The `waterways` variable violates the exclusion restriction because rivers and streams also served as boundaries for separately governed school districts and municipalities, and jurisdictional fragmentation directly alters city public spending responsibilities and fiscal competition independent of racial segregation. The `audit_grant` variable is randomly assigned and satisfies the exclusion restriction because funds went to nonprofits rather than city governments, but it is defined for only 40 cities and has a first-stage F-statistic of about 2, making it too weak for reliable inference. Instead, I recommend a two-way fixed effects panel design across the 1980, 1990, 2000, and 2010 census waves, regressing city direct general expenditure per resident on the multigroup entropy segregation index while including city fixed effects and state-by-year fixed effects. To mitigate time-varying confounding, the specification should control for city covariates (`log_pop`, `pct_black`, `pct_hisp`, `med_income`, and `own_rate`), though demographic and economic controls that may be endogenous to segregation should be introduced sequentially to check sensitivity. The main threat to this strategy is time-varying unobserved shocks—such as local economic shifts or sorting dynamics—that simultaneously drive within-city changes in residential segregation and municipal spending.

Neither candidate instrument in the dataset supports a credible instrumental variables strategy to estimate the effect of racial residential segregation on city direct general expenditure per resident. First, `waterways` (the count of rivers and streams crossing the city) has a strong first stage, but the program documentation notes that every stream in the 1920 boundary survey became a municipal or school district boundary line. Because jurisdictional fragmentation directly alters fiscal competition and the division of spending responsibilities across local governments, `waterways` violates the exclusion restriction. Second, `audit_grant` (the 1990 random assignment of fair-housing testing grants to nonprofits) satisfies independence and exclusion, as it was randomly drawn and affected nothing else in the city. However, `audit_grant` is only defined for 40 cities and yields a first-stage F-statistic of about 2, making it far too weak for valid two-stage least squares inference. Consequently, no valid and sufficiently strong instrument is available in the data, and you should instead rely on a panel fixed-effects design controlling for city and state-by-year fixed effects alongside time-varying covariates (`log_pop`, `pct_black`, `pct_hisp`, `med_income`, and `own_rate`), while acknowledging that time-varying unobserved shocks to local demographics and public finances remain the main threat to identification.

I recommend against an instrumental-variables design because neither candidate instrument in the dataset provides a credible basis for identification. The `waterways` variable (following the Hoxby-style stream-boundary logic) violates the exclusion restriction because rivers and streams also fragment metropolitan areas into more separately governed municipalities and school districts—and require bridge and flood infrastructure—which directly alters city direct general expenditure per resident independent of racial segregation. The `audit_grant` variable comes from a federal random draw that paid nonprofits rather than city governments and satisfies the exclusion restriction, but it is defined for only 40 cities and has a first-stage F-statistic of about 2, making it far too weak and underpowered for reliable inference. Instead, we should exploit the 1980–2010 panel structure using a two-way fixed-effects specification with city fixed effects and state-by-year fixed effects, controlling for time-varying covariates (`log_pop`, `pct_black`, `pct_hisp`, `med_income`, and `own_rate`) and clustering standard errors at the city level. If you still wish to report an experimental benchmark on the 40-city subsample, we should report the reduced-form intent-to-treat effect of `audit_grant` in post-1990 waves alongside weak-instrument-robust Anderson–Rubin confidence intervals rather than standard 2SLS. The main threat to the panel fixed-effects strategy is time-varying unobserved within-city shocks—such as suburbanization, industrial decline, or local fiscal crises—that simultaneously reshape residential sorting and municipal budgets.

audit_grant | plausible

To estimate the causal effect of racial residential segregation on city direct general expenditure per resident, I propose an instrumental variables (2SLS) design following the topographic approach of Ananat (2011) and Trounstine (2016). We will instrument for the multigroup entropy segregation index using `waterways`, the number of rivers and streams crossing the city, which naturally divide neighborhoods and raise the segregation index by 1.5 points per waterway on average. Following the codebook specification, the model will include state-by-year fixed effects and control for `log_pop`, while we can assess robustness using predetermined demographic and economic covariates (`pct_black`, `pct_hisp`, `med_income`, `own_rate`) with standard errors clustered at the city level. I considered an alternative instrument, `audit_grant` (a 1990 randomized fair-housing audit grant), but rejected it because it is only defined for 40 large cities in two states and suffers from a weak first stage ($F \approx 2$). The main threat to the `waterways` identification strategy is a violation of the exclusion restriction: rivers and streams may directly increase local public spending per resident by requiring more infrastructure, such as bridges, flood control, and fragmented service delivery, independent of racial segregation.

CANDIDATES:
waterways | plausible
audit_grant | doubtful
